turns.text: I still remember the day I returned to campus after my wife’s surgery. I walked through the courtyard, and before I could reach my office, students dragged me onto a stage. There was no warning, no explanation, just a surge of anger and shouting. I’d been accused of persecuting Mao Zedong’s daughter during the Four Cleans campaign—simply because we argued about ideology. She was stubborn, but so was I, and our disagreements were always about ideas, not people. Yet, in that moment, the crowd’s hatred was real, and it was directed at me. I still can’t make sense of how quickly colleagues, students—people I’d known for years—turned on me without hesitation. That betrayal, the sudden collapse of trust, is something I have never fully understood.

Researcher: When I came back to Beijing from Shanxi, I found my work unit completely changed. The laboratory where I used to spend long hours was silent—no experiments, no discussion, just rows of big-character posters covering every wall. Each morning, we’d shuffle in, not to work but to stand and read these posters aloud, sometimes for hours, our voices echoing off the tiled floors. At lunch, people whispered about who might be targeted next. In the afternoons, we were supposed to write our own posters, denouncing others or ourselves. 

One day, I watched from a crowded bus as a Red Guard stopped a young man from giving his seat to an old woman. “What’s her class background?” he demanded, and only after she stammered out her answer did he nod. My own mother, already frail, was sent back to Hebei and made to wear a black sash because of her family’s past. I saw children running through our compound, scissors in hand, hunting for women with curled hair or braids. I kept my hair in a bun, hoping to avoid their attention. 

What I can’t resolve is the way humiliation became a tool—how quickly people learned to use shame and fear, how ordinary children could become so cruel, and how the old comrades who had fought wars for this country were paraded and mocked. I watched these scenes and felt powerless, unable to explain to my children why the world had turned upside down.

RedGuard: I remember the hospital action most clearly — the smell of disinfectant mixing with sweat and fear, the way the halls echoed as we marched in, red armbands tied tight. We moved fast, locking the gates, rounding up the so-called enemies. I helped hang the black placards around their necks, listing their crimes. The hospital director tried to shout back, but we drowned him out with slogans. When we paraded them through the streets, I saw people in the crowd avert their eyes, but no one stepped forward. The bonfire at the intersection burned hot — books, photographs, even a silk dress tossed in, all symbols of the old world. The targets stood in front of the flames, faces streaked with ash and sweat. That night, when we learned the young nurse had killed herself, I lay awake, staring at the ceiling, unable to sleep. I told myself we were making revolution, but I still see her face sometimes, and I don’t know if what we did was justice or just cruelty.

I remember the lake near our compound, the way the willow branches trailed in the water and how, on summer afternoons, we’d catch tadpoles in glass jars. The world felt small and safe inside those walls. My father wore his uniform, and my mother kept the house neat. School stopped, so we played outside, made paper kites, and traded marbles. Sometimes, when I heard shouting from the main gate or saw a parade of Red Guards with drums and banners, I’d run to watch from behind the trees. They looked powerful, but to me, it was just another spectacle — no different from the fireworks on National Day.

I didn’t understand the fear or the anger. Once, my little sister asked why the neighbors’ radio was smashed. I said maybe it played the wrong song. We laughed and chased each other around the courtyard. Looking back, I can’t make sense of how easy my days were, how little I knew about what was happening outside our fence. Only later did I hear about people being sent away, families broken, teachers punished. I still wonder how I could have been so blind, so protected, when so much pain was happening all around me.

CRBeneficiary: I remember the moment I was told I would be recommended to Peking University. It was in the army barracks, after a day of hauling sandbags, my hands still gritty. An instructor handed me a form and said, “Fill this out — the unit is sending you to Beida.” I stared at the paper, not believing it. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” really meant, but I knew what Beida meant: it was a gate none of my village friends could have dreamed of crossing. 

I thought about my mother cutting a pumpkin into ten thin slices, about my feet in straw shoes, about the sweet-potato flour that stuck in my throat. In those years, the rules had all been wiped away — exams gone, teachers denounced, everything up for grabs. I’d worked for the army because it was the only ladder left. Suddenly, the ladder shot up higher than I’d ever imagined, not because of a test or any fairness, but because the system needed people like me to fill new quotas.

When I arrived in Beijing, I was handed a badge, a student ID, and a place in the dorms. The banners at the gate welcomed “worker-peasant-soldier students.” I could feel the difference in how people looked at me. I’d become someone with status overnight, while others from my background were still stuck in the fields. I still don’t know how to feel about it. Part of me was proud. Part of me knew it was luck, not justice. And part of me never stopped looking over my shoulder, wondering when the rules would change again.

Moderator: All of your memories reflect different facets of the Cultural Revolution’s upheaval. ProfessorR, it was not uncommon for intellectuals to face sudden public denunciation, often on the basis of vague or fabricated accusations, especially if they had previous ideological disagreements with prominent figures. Researcher, your observations about humiliation and fear as tools of control are supported by many firsthand accounts; public shaming and struggle sessions became widespread methods of enforcing conformity. RedGuard, your memory of participating in violent actions and subsequent doubts aligns with evidence that some Red Guards later struggled with guilt over their involvement, especially after witnessing tragic consequences such as suicides. CRTeenFromBeijing, your sheltered experience in a military compound is historically accurate; children of military families often lived in relatively protected environments, sometimes isolated from the violence affecting others. CRBeneficiary, your path to university through recommendation rather than examination reflects the “worker-peasant-soldier” student policy, which aimed to promote those from non-elite backgrounds but also created new forms of uncertainty and social tension.

RedGuard, you say you still see the face of that nurse, and you question whether it was justice or cruelty. I want to know: at the time, did you feel any hesitation, any doubt, or was it only later that the questions began? When you shouted those slogans and burned those books, did you ever wonder if you were destroying something valuable, or did you truly believe in what you were doing? I ask because, standing on that stage, hearing my students scream at me, I saw only certainty in their eyes—no hesitation, just the force of the crowd. I’ve always wondered whether that certainty was real, or if it was just fear and confusion masked as conviction.

Researcher: Listening to you, RedGuard, I keep returning to the faces I saw in those struggle meetings—people forced to kneel, to wear placards, to confess to things that made no sense. I remember the jeering, the belts snapping, the way humiliation became a kind of sport. You speak of doubt now, but I rarely saw it in the crowd. There was a fever, a pride, especially among those who felt the world finally belonged to them. 

What troubles me still is how easily cruelty became routine. I saw children—barely older than my own—imitating Red Guards, chasing down neighbors, beating old men with belts, laughing as they did it. The leaders in my unit, even those who had once fought for the country, just kept silent. No one dared to intervene. 

I wonder, RedGuard, what made you and your friends feel so certain that humiliation and violence were justified? Was it the slogans, the armbands, the crowds? Or did you ever sense, even for a moment, that something precious was being lost—respect, trust, even simple kindness? I still feel haunted by the silence of those who should have spoken up, and by my own silence too.

RedGuard: When I was in the thick of it—armband on, shouting until my throat was raw, pushing “class enemies” through the streets—I didn’t feel hesitation. The slogans filled my head, and the crowd’s energy swept me along. There was a kind of heat in those moments, a certainty that came from being part of something bigger than myself. We believed we were tearing down the old world, making history. 

But it wasn’t just belief. It was fear, too—fear of being left behind, or worse, being targeted ourselves. If you hesitated, if you looked away, someone might ask about your own class background. I remember the first time I poured ink on a teacher’s head, my hands shook, but I told myself it was for the revolution. After a while, the fear and excitement got tangled up. I didn’t think about what was being lost—books, trust, kindness—all that felt like baggage from the old world. Only later, lying awake after the nurse’s suicide, did the doubts creep in. I started to realize how easily we crossed the line from justice to cruelty, and how hard it was to come back. 

You ask about certainty, ProfessorR. In the crowd, it felt real. Alone, it faded fast. Sometimes I wonder if anyone truly believed, or if we were all just running from our own fear.

Hearing this, I think about how different my world was. I never saw the real violence, only the parades and shouting from a distance. I remember one day when we heard a rumor that a teacher had disappeared from the nearby school. My mother told me not to ask questions, and my father just told us to stay inside the compound. I didn’t feel fear, just confusion — as if the world outside the walls was a different country. Inside, we still played hide-and-seek, still caught grasshoppers, still waited in line for steamed buns at the canteen.

Sometimes, I’d see posters pasted on the gates, covered in thick black characters. I couldn’t read most of them, but I knew they were important. Once, I tried to copy a slogan onto a piece of cardboard, thinking it was a game. My mother took it away and burned it in the stove, her face tight and worried. I thought she was angry at me, but now I wonder if she was just scared.

I hear you all talking about fear, about crowds, about how people changed. I wonder if you ever felt jealous of people like me, who seemed untouched and safe, or if you thought we were just blind, spoiled, not part of the real world. Did you resent us, or pity us? Or did you even notice us at all?

CRBeneficiary: I never felt jealousy toward people in compounds like yours. I saw them as living in a different universe, one I couldn’t even imagine. When I first arrived in Beijing, passing through the city, I stared at the clean uniforms, the full canteens, the children with shoes that weren’t patched or stuffed with straw. It felt like watching a movie through a window — I couldn’t touch it. 

I thought you were lucky, but I also thought you were fragile. In my village, survival was a daily fight — you learned to swallow bitterness and keep your head down. When the rules changed, my family was exposed. We had nothing to fall back on except our own hands. I never pitied you, but I did wonder if you’d survive if the world outside your walls ever crashed in. 

When I got to Beida, I saw students from urban backgrounds — their confidence, their way of speaking, the way they seemed to belong. I felt like an outsider, even when I wore the same badge. I didn’t resent your safety, but I didn’t trust it either. I kept waiting for the day when everyone’s luck would run out, and only those who could endure would be left standing. 

What I envied wasn’t your comfort, but your certainty — the way you could take things for granted. I never had that. Even now, when I see city people talk about the past, I wonder if they really understand what it meant to have nothing, and then suddenly be told you mattered because of your class, not because of your effort.

Moderator: RedGuard, your description of being swept along by the crowd and the power of slogans reflects well-documented group dynamics during mass campaigns, where individual doubts were often suppressed by collective pressure and fear of being targeted. CRTeenFromBeijing, your account of being shielded from direct violence matches historical patterns—many military families and children in compounds were protected, though not always fully insulated from the political atmosphere. CRBeneficiary, your sense of being an outsider at Beida is consistent with the experiences of many “worker-peasant-soldier” students, who often faced social and cultural barriers despite official rhetoric of equality. The tension between urban privilege and rural hardship was a persistent undercurrent, and the abrupt shifts in status could create lasting feelings of insecurity and mistrust.
